title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters

understand.question: Given a text string, what is the length of the longest unbroken stretch of characters in which every character appears at most once?
understand.plainExplanation: Imagine highlighting a contiguous snippet of letters with a marker. You want your highlight to be as wide as possible, but the moment a character would appear twice inside the highlight, you must shrink the left side past its earlier copy.
understand.inputMeaning: A string s made of English letters, digits, symbols, or spaces (including an empty string "").
understand.outputMeaning: An integer equal to the maximum length of any valid substring with all unique characters.
rules: A substring must be contiguous (you cannot delete characters from the middle).
Case matters ('a' and 'A' are different characters), and spaces/symbols count as characters.
An empty string "" has a longest unique substring of length 0.

terms.definition: A contiguous slice s[left..right] of consecutive characters from s.
Two pointers [left, right] that expand right to include new items and advance left only when a rule (here: uniqueness) is broken.
A map storing the most recent position where each character appeared so left can jump past duplicates in one step.

example1.whyValid: The substring "cadbz" (indices 0..4) has 5 distinct characters. When index 5 ('a') arrives, 'a' repeats from index 1, so left slides to 2 ("dbza"), and later reaches "zabcd" (also length 5), so the maximum length is 5.

example2.whyEdgeCase: Trap for naive index jumps! When right reaches the second 'a' at index 3, the old 'a' was at index 0, which is ALREADY behind left = 2. Never move left backwards: always use left = max(left, lastSeen[ch] + 1).

steps.title: Indices 0..4: expand across unique letters 'c','a','d','b','z'
steps.description: None of c, a, d, b, z is in our active window [0..4]. Record each index in lastSeen and update maxLen = 5.

steps.title: Index 5 ('a'): duplicate inside window -> jump L to 2
steps.description: lastSeen['a'] is 1 (>= L = 0). Move L to 1 + 1 = 2 so the old 'a' leaves the window. Update lastSeen['a'] = 5. Window is "dbza" (length 4).

steps.title: Indices 6..8 ('b', 'c', 'd'): slide past 'b', ignore stale 'c', 'd'
steps.description: At R=6 ('b'), lastSeen['b']=3 >= L=2 so L jumps to 4. At R=7 ('c') and R=8 ('d'), their old indices (0 and 2) are < L=4 so L stays at 4! Window "zabcd" reaches length 5. Return 5.

state.caption: Window [4..8] = "zabcd" also has length 5. Final answer: 5.

approaches.name: Brute Force with Character Set
approaches.coreIdeaSummary: Start from each index i and extend right until a repeat occurs.
approaches.coreIdea: For every starting index i, grow the substring rightwards using a set until encountering a repeated character.
steps: For each start index i, create an empty seen set.
Loop j from i to n - 1: if s[j] is in seen, break; else insert s[j] and update best.
approaches.whyItWorks: Checking every possible start index and stopping on the first duplicate examines every valid unique substring.
approaches.whenToUse: Only for tiny strings or baseline verification.

complexity.variables: n = string length, sigma = character alphabet size

approaches.name: Sliding Window with Active Set
approaches.coreIdeaSummary: Shrink left one step at a time while s[right] is in the active set.
approaches.coreIdea: Maintain a set of characters inside [left..right]. Before adding s[right], advance left and remove s[left] until s[right] is no longer present.
steps: Initialize left = 0, best = 0, and an empty set active.
For right from 0 to n - 1: while s[right] is in active, remove s[left] and increment left.
Add s[right] to active and update best = max(best, right - left + 1).
approaches.whyItWorks: Each character is inserted once and removed at most once, so left and right together make at most 2n moves.
approaches.whenToUse: Easy-to-adapt template for sliding window problems with frequency constraints.

complexity.variables: n = string length, sigma = alphabet size

approaches.name: Sliding Window with Last-Seen Map
approaches.recommendedTradeOff: Visits each index strictly once by jumping left directly past the previous occurrence instead of deleting elements step by step.
approaches.coreIdeaSummary: Store each character's latest index and jump left = max(left, lastSeen[ch] + 1).
approaches.coreIdea: Track the last index where every character appeared. When s[right] was seen at prev >= left, move left directly to prev + 1.
steps: For each right from 0 to n - 1: if s[right] is in lastSeen and lastSeen[s[right]] >= left, set left = lastSeen[s[right]] + 1.
Store lastSeen[s[right]] = right and update best = max(best, right - left + 1).
approaches.whyItWorks: Taking max(left, prev + 1) keeps left monotonic so stale characters from before the current window are safely ignored without removing them.
approaches.whenToUse: Default optimal solution for general Unicode or ASCII strings.

complexity.variables: n = string length, sigma = alphabet size

approaches.name: Fixed 128-Slot ASCII Array
approaches.coreIdeaSummary: Replace the hash map with a 128-element integer array for ASCII inputs.
approaches.coreIdea: For standard ASCII strings, use a fixed int[128] array initialized to -1 to achieve worst-case O(1) lookup without hashing.
steps: Initialize int[128] lastSeen filled with -1, left = 0, best = 0.
For each character code code = ord(s[right]), set left = max(left, lastSeen[code] + 1).
Set lastSeen[code] = right and update best = max(best, right - left + 1).
approaches.whyItWorks: Since ASCII codes fall in 0..127, direct array indexing avoids hash collisions and dynamic allocation.
approaches.whenToUse: When inputs are guaranteed to be ASCII and strict worst-case O(n) time / O(1) fixed table space is desired.
